title: Reference notebook template
text:
Lab 02 is the visual and interaction prototype for this template. Lab 00 and Lab 01 use the same opening and outer frame. Further chapter implementation should follow this template after its rendered experience has been reviewed; older notebooks are not interchangeable visual examples.


Show the destination and route before the first experiment. Use the same visible labels in each lab:

Your scenario: a short scene from the continuing project, the decision due today, and a photograph that makes the setting tangible. Use the shared notebook_scenario(...) helper after the title and project selector, before the learning goals. Reuse the MLSysIM episode or canonical lab narrative; do not maintain a second scene in the notebook.
What you will learn: a short set of observable chapter-owned goals, expressed as things students can compare, explain, or defend. Name the ability without announcing the experimental finding.
Your route through this lab: every part’s title, question, and contribution to the decision; mark the current part. Keep later parts visible even when their instruments are not yet available.
What you will hand in: one integrated discussion and its required evidence; explain what a supported submission contains.
What comes next: the next part and next lab question, and what evidence carries forward. A preview is not a claim that the student has already established that evidence.

Reveal consequences and deeper explanations progressively, not the learning goals, route, submission requirements, or destination. Keep section headings and short previews visible from the start. Unavailable controls should state what action opens them. Optional background can collapse; the core learning goals cannot.
Within each investigation, use a narrative learning cycle:
Scene → short briefing → meaningful choice → consequence feedback → explanation → handoff.
Give students enough to understand the task, terms, and starting conditions before acting. The concept map’s learning claim and misconception are authoring guidance; avoid revealing their resolution in the opening. After a choice, show what actually changed, the competing consequence, and any failure or unknown. Invite an explanation and a further trial, then connect the result to the next decision. Feedback is more than a verdict: its content depends on the saved comparison and remains available after an incorrect prediction. The shared narrative contract defines progressive disclosure and feedback requirements.
Use the same sequence in every chapter lab:
Project → Your scenario → Learning goals and route → Investigate → Discuss and submit → Next.
The opening identifies the chosen system, gives the catalog-owned episode event, and states the chapter’s observable goal. Use notebook_bridge(...) for the familiar connection strip. “Previously” describes the project thread; only verified compatible records may be described as prior supporting evidence. Otherwise identify the supplied starting case. Orientation uses Start / Goal / Next and rehearses the interfaces instead of making a deployment claim.
Keep a short core investigation and optional depth in the same places. Let students choose a useful contrast before opening “Help me design a comparison.” Its Look at / Compare / Explain / Challenge entries offer attention, a route, the mechanism, and a transfer probe. Numeric outcomes, failed gates, units, and evidence limitations remain visible without requesting help.
The closing team decision uses saved compatible evidence. It names the claim or hold, rejected alternative, unresolved obligation, and reversal condition. Finish with visible Carry forward / Still open / Next labels; the next chapter question must be as recognizable as the opening goal. A complete discussion is not automatic mastery or permission to deploy.
The filled interaction and acceptance contract is in the Volume I engagement specification.
The opening tells students what just happened and why a decision is needed now. Use natural language such as “Save your progress” and “Download your work.” Keep internal payload names, file schemas, and storage implementation details out of the story. Technical concepts such as a belief state or data lineage remain precise where the chapter teaches them.
Use the shared packaged project photograph, with meaningful alt text and a short caption. Keep source, license, and image modifications in the photo credit. The photograph illustrates the project setting; it is not a measurement of the named product. Images must work without a separate image-host request.
Every lab ends with the H2 Discuss and submit, rendered by notebook_submission(...) outside completion gates. Explain how to use the actual download controls and submit through the course system. Provide a readable discussion alongside structured evidence. Orientation uses orientation=True and saves the project choice and practice work. Do not promise automatic submission, file import, or a dedicated print interface.



Read the chapter and its concept map. State the core claims, the consequential choices students will explore, what stays fixed, the observations they need, and the discussion they will submit. Choose instruments for those purposes. The chapter determines the experiment; the shared template organizes it.
For Volume I, the shared lab learning contract anchors this work in exploring tradeoffs. Every notebook has a matching vol1/concepts/<notebook_stem>_concepts.yml file. Its distilled concepts name the chapter source and owner, learning claim, misconception, tradeoff, student action, evidence view, and explanation requirement. These are authoring and assessment fields; they do not require separate student essays.
Bind those concepts to the selected MLSysIM mission’s chapter episode and engine/data/deployment_learning/<track>.json investigations. Preserve the same conceptual goal across tracks while changing the task, meaningful choices, observations, and consequences to fit the actual project. The complete paradigm guides write out those bindings. Run python labs/tools/check_lab_concepts.py and the narrative generator’s --check before extending a notebook. Consistency checks do not establish numerical fidelity or student learning.



Orientation selects a deployment project within TinyML, MobileML, EdgeML, or CloudML. Show its user, input, intended outcome, deployed endpoint, and unresolved requirements. Obtain the versioned mission and chapter episode from MLSysIM; do not replace it with an unrelated scenario when the next notebook opens. Keep the category visible so a memorable project does not erase the hierarchy.
Each chapter is an episode in that project. State the decision due now, what earlier work contributes, and what new evidence this chapter adds. A wearable can use a separate development host for training; a cloud project stays within the single-endpoint scope of this volume. State that boundary in the mission. Controlled teaching fixtures are not measurements of the project or a named commercial product. Never disguise a generic fixture as product validation.
Persist project identity separately from experimental evidence. The deployment dossier accumulates scoped decisions and unresolved obligations. A previous passing experiment is reusable only when its task, artifact, population, and measurement conditions match. A missing earlier record means a labeled standalone start, not a fabricated history. Comparing another track must not relabel earlier saved results.



Use mlsysbook_labs.notebook for explicit layout containers. Apply notebook_shell(...) to the opening, tabbed investigations, discussion export, and status. They share a centered maximum width and the same edges. Let prose use a shorter reading measure inside that frame. Do not make a full-window hero above a narrow worksheet or match CSS against an inline background string.
The opening contains a small lab/chapter label, title, one driving question, short concept labels, and context selector. Core learning goals, the route, deliverable, and next-step preview remain visible. Supporting reading, detailed background, and assumptions can use an accordion. The first meaningful action should appear without scrolling through a second chapter of prose. Orientation is a short interface rehearsal; it does not need technical instruments or a physics failure to look like the chapter labs.
from mlsysbook_labs.notebook import (
    notebook_header, notebook_shell, notebook_part, notebook_workspace,
    notebook_cards, notebook_progress, notebook_status, notebook_table,
)

notebook_shell([
    notebook_header(metadata, driving_question, topics=core_concept_labels),
    context_control,
    mo.accordion({"Reading and assumptions": reading_and_assumptions}),
])
These helpers own presentation only. Physical quantities, scenario values, model behavior, and sweep points come from MLSysIM. Use its formatters for the returned quantities. Leave legacy global CSS out of these opt-in reference notebooks so its width heuristics do not compete with the explicit frame.



Use a structured prediction before revealing instruments. Any submitted prediction unlocks exploration. Once committed, replace the tall form with a concise prediction and observation; keep the original prediction in the saved comparison. Correctness must not gate exploration or completion.
Within a part, use notebook_workspace(controls, results) to keep controls beside the linked instrument on a wide screen and above it on a narrow screen. Give the learner a clear question and a consequential action. Keep action buttons adjacent and in order: pin a run, change a choice, save a contrast. Place status and a short next-step hint nearby.
A prediction is only the opening question. Each part needs a connected investigation: diagnose the baseline, design a purposeful comparison, test a boundary or an ineffective remedy, explain the mechanism, and consider a changed condition. Choose the moves the chapter claim needs; do not fill a question quota. Titles and prompts must not announce the answer before the prediction. Keep deeper probes optional when they would overload the core.
Collect a short causal interpretation tied to the saved comparison. When a comparison changes, require the learner to revisit its interpretation instead of silently attaching old prose to new evidence. Transfer claims remain predictions until the student actually runs the changed condition. A sequence of green checks or any two different settings is not evidence of understanding.
Use the same state vocabulary throughout:

Live experiment: follows the controls and can change.
Pinned comparison: retains a run while the learner tries another choice.
Saved evidence: an immutable comparison consumed by later decisions.
Stale evidence: retained history whose upstream assumptions have changed.

Use reactive notebook capabilities where they clarify the concept: linked charts, current and pinned markers, changing budget boundaries, capacity views, dependency traces, and evidence-dependent downstream experiments. Editable code or chart selection is optional; add it only when it supports a learning goal. Do not make a table of calculated answers the default instrument for every part.
The Lab 02 prototype demonstrates these choices:

Locality uses a linked latency decomposition and an ideal-processor contrast.
Resources show required versus available capacity before timing; an overflowed configuration has no executable timing bar.
Operation uses sourced energy and power curves, an observation boundary, current/pinned markers, and separate service, energy, and power verdicts.
Placement shows the supplied gates in a compact matrix. Excluded candidates remain visible, and unavailable evidence stays unresolved.




Show the active constraint or evidence gap beside the result, with text as well as color. Use notebook_cards(...) for a small set of consequential outcomes. Use a single concise prediction/observation comparison instead of repeating several full-width information banners.
Keep Calculation Notes, exact data rows, and deeper explanations expandable. Small read-only evidence tables use notebook_table(...); use mo.ui.table when sorting, selecting, or inspecting a larger dataset is part of the task. Avoid search, column management, and per-table downloads when they do not help the investigation. The discussion export already carries the evidence.



The discussion workspace summarizes saved and stale evidence, provides usable writing fields, and asks for the decision, mechanism, rejected alternative, uncertainty, and revisit condition. It should remain possible to justify a hold or retain the baseline.
Generate the downloadable discussion from valid saved comparisons and the student’s text. Keep download readiness separate from persistent-save status. An explicit Save discussion action records the completed discussion; editing afterward must require saving again. Do not silently mark every draft keystroke as a final saved discussion. On a storage error, keep the report available and show an honest unavailable state.
Keep the footer quiet and aligned with the frame. Show the context and actual evidence/save state. Internal API names, schema versions, and implementation provenance belong in source and exported metadata, not the opening banner.



Inspect native Marimo and the exported browser notebook. Check a wide desktop, laptop, tablet, and narrow phone viewport. Check the locked and unlocked states, not only an initial screenshot.
Verify that the opening, context, tabs, instruments, report, and footer align; controls remain associated with their results when columns stack; and labels, legends, tables, and tabs do not clip. Check that a first-time student can reach the first prediction with reading details collapsed. Inspect keyboard use and mobile scrolling rather than assuming an absence of document overflow proves usability.
Exercise a wrong prediction, pin and change controls, save a contrast, invalidate an upstream choice, generate the discussion, save deliberately, edit again, download, reload, and simulate unavailable storage. Rebuild the browser wheels after helper or model changes. Source checks, browser checks, and student pilots answer different questions; report them separately.
Use simulated student, instructor, and classroom walkthroughs to identify likely problems, revise, and review the actual revision again. Label their observations as simulated. Real student feedback requires an actual pilot: observe independent use, ask learners to explain a saved comparison and a new case, review the exported reasoning, and record confusing controls and stalls. Do not claim engagement, completion time, or learning gains from agent reviews.
Run the relevant notebook reference tests and the static/style checks, then the lab suite after integration:
python3 -m pytest labs/tests/test_placement_reference.py labs/tests/test_static.py
python3 labs/tools/check_browser_wheels.py
python3 -m pytest labs/tests
For Lab 02, run labs/tools/check_placement_discussion.py --url URL against the running native or exported notebook. It exercises actual reactive callbacks: attach, edit, recapture, reattach, download, explicitly save, and edit again. Headless app.run() checks do not exercise the same event loop. A browser walkthrough caught an attachment state bug that the reference tests missed.


Maintain one notebook per chapter. A track selects its canonical MLSysIM project narrative, workload, resource profile, constraints, and supported experiments together. TinyML, MobileML, EdgeML, and CloudML share the chapter concept set and investigation components. A workload case, such as a larger model, is a controlled variation within that track, not a separate notebook or a substitute for a distinct deployment context.
After a prediction, changing an experiment control updates live evidence and consequence feedback immediately. Reserve explicit actions for pinning a comparison, recording a decision, and downloading work. Keep saved evidence distinct from live evidence. A track change must not attach the previous track’s notes or decisions to the new project.
Use the volume’s book accent for headings, links, and navigation; retain semantic resource and outcome colors for instruments. The published lab should retain shared course navigation, a return-to-chapter link, and previous/next lab links around a compact notebook workspace. A downloadable standalone notebook should remain usable without that site shell.



The laboratory index uses the shared Quarto navigation and ecosystem styles. Each lab opens as a full-page Marimo notebook, without an iframe or nested course page. The build reuses the actual Quarto header and compiled theme from the landing page: shared shield, brand, ecosystem menus, and responsive navigation. A quiet contextual row adds the lab index, volume/chapter context, reading link, and previous/next labs from the canonical learning catalog. There is no separately authored notebook masthead. Quarto styles are scoped to the header so they cannot change Marimo widgets. Preserve the book’s fonts and volume accents; reserve the remaining viewport for the notebook. Keep notebook CSS scoped so it cannot restyle the course navigation.
The reference example demonstrates this shell around an interactive investigation. Production Marimo integration must preserve this shell around the notebook workspace; a standalone downloaded notebook can omit site navigation.

title: MLSysBook Interactive Modes & Tooling Catalog
text:
Version: 1.0.0 Target Environment: Marimo Reactive Notebooks (marimo >= 0.11.0) & MLSysBook Web/WASM Runtime Core Framework: Python 3.11+, Plotly Graph Objects (plotly.graph_objects), mlsysim, mlsysbook_labs





Executive Overview & Pedagogical Philosophy
Category 1: Input & Control Devices

1.1 Continuous Value Sliders
1.2 Discrete Step & Exponential Sliders
1.3 Dual-Thumb Range Sliders
1.4 Radio Button Groups & Mutually Exclusive Pickers
1.5 Dropdown Selectors
1.6 Multi-Select Pills & Checkbox Groups
1.7 Toggle Switches & Boolean Flags
1.8 Action & Event Trigger Buttons
1.9 Form Submitters & Batch Checkpoint Enclosures
1.10 Numeric Precision Inputs
1.11 Freeform Engineering Decision Logs

Category 2: Analytical Visualizations & Trade-Off Surfaces

2.1 Dynamic Pareto Frontiers
2.2 Williams Roofline Model Charts
2.3 Waterfall Latency & Energy Decomposition Bars
2.4 Radar / Spider Multi-Axis System Trade-Off Charts
2.5 2D Feasibility & Contingency Heatmaps
2.6 Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) Tail-Latency Curves
2.7 Interactive Telemetry DataFrames & Margin Tables
2.8 Hardware Topology & Pipeline Execution Flow Diagrams

Category 3: Pedagogical & Feedback Mechanisms

3.1 Prediction Locks with mo.stop
3.2 Productive Failure Redouts & Visceral Alert Callouts
3.3 Calculation Notes & MathPeek Physics Accordions
3.4 Multi-Track Perspective Switchers
3.5 Design Ledger State Persistence & Audit Logging

Cross-Cutting Interaction Matrix





The MLSysBook interactive curriculum rejects passive notebook reading. Systems engineering cannot be mastered through static code cells or linear prose because systems are defined by coupling, constraints, and non-linear multi-dimensional trade-off spaces.
When an engineer scales batch size, latency does not simply drop; memory spills, cache lines thrash, and queueing delays spike at the 99th percentile. When precision is quantized from FP16 to INT4, memory bandwidth bottlenecks ease, but kernel dequantization overheads arise and catastrophic numerical divergence looms.
To teach this intuition, our Marimo labs adhere to four strict design tenets: 1. Predict Before Observing (Gated Cognitive Friction): Students must record a hypothesis before simulation instrumentation renders. Free-wheeling widget twiddling without prior mental commitment breeds false fluency. 2. Visceral Productive Failure: Hitting a hardware thermal ceiling, an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) panic, or an SLA deadline violation must trigger clear, unignorable feedback (shaking redouts, cliff graphs) that directly exposes the binding physical constraint. 3. Multi-Perspective Grounding (The 4 Archetypes): Every concept is evaluated through four distinct industry archetypes: - Cloud Supercomputing: Scale-out H100/H200 clusters, SLA cliffs, multi-tenant throughput, energy megawatts. - Edge & Embodied AI: NVIDIA Drive Orin / Jetson, sub-10ms hard real-time safety, rare-hazard perception. - Mobile SoC: Apple Silicon / Qualcomm Snapdragon NPU, unified memory, thermal throttling envelopes. - TinyML & Microcontrollers: ARM Cortex-M55 / ESP32-S3, strict <512 KB SRAM limits, micro-watt energy harvesting. 4. Traceable Architectural Accounting: Every design choice updates an immutable Design Ledger, teaching students to defend decisions with empirical telemetry and Iron Law accounting.

Dynamic Multi-Objective Pareto Frontier



go.Scatter(x=..., y=..., mode='markers+lines') with convex-hull or non-dominated sorting logic.



Use to demonstrate that in real-world ML systems, there are no unilateral optimizations—only trade-offs along an optimal boundary. Any point below/behind the frontier is sub-optimal; any point beyond it is physically impossible under current technology constraints.




X-Axis: Cost Metric (Latency in ms, Energy in Joules, Dollar Cost $/1M tokens, or SRAM footprint in KB).
Y-Axis: Quality Metric (Top-1 Accuracy %, BLEU/ROUGE score, Safety Margin %).
Marker Color/Size: Secondary trade-off (e.g., Model Parameter Scale or Peak Thermal Dissipation).
Frontier Line: Step-wise or convex hull connecting non-dominated operating configurations.




import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

def build_pareto_frontier(models, active_point):
    # Sort models by latency
    sorted_models = sorted(models, key=lambda m: m['latency_ms'])
    pareto_x, pareto_y = [], []
    max_acc = -1.0
    for m in sorted_models:
        if m['accuracy_pct'] > max_acc:
            pareto_x.append(m['latency_ms'])
            pareto_y.append(m['accuracy_pct'])
            max_acc = m['accuracy_pct']

    fig = go.Figure()
    # Non-dominated frontier
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=pareto_x, y=pareto_y,
        mode='lines',
        name='Pareto Frontier',
        line=dict(color='#A51C30', width=2, dash='dash')
    ))
    # All candidate architectural designs
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[m['latency_ms'] for m in models],
        y=[m['accuracy_pct'] for m in models],
        mode='markers+text',
        text=[m['name'] for m in models],
        textposition='top right',
        marker=dict(size=10, color='#1F407A', opacity=0.7),
        name='Architectural Candidates'
    ))
    # Currently evaluated student design
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[active_point['latency_ms']],
        y=[active_point['accuracy_pct']],
        mode='markers',
        marker=dict(size=16, color='#247A4D', symbol='star', line=dict(width=2, color='white')),
        name='Your Active Design'
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        title="Accuracy vs. Latency Pareto Surface",
        xaxis=dict(title="P99 Inference Latency (ms) [Lower is Better]"),
        yaxis=dict(title="Downstream Task Accuracy (%) [Higher is Better]"),
        template="plotly_white",
        height=380,
    )
    return fig







Williams Operational Roofline Model



go.Scatter(..., x=..., y=..., mode='lines') on dual logarithmic axes (\(\log_{10} - \log_{10}\)) with dynamic design point diamonds.



The foundational visualization for hardware-software co-design (Labs 02, 05, 10, 11). Quantifies whether a workload is Memory-Bandwidth Bound or Peak-Compute Bound based on its Arithmetic Intensity (\(I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{Byte}\)).




X-Axis: Arithmetic Intensity (\(\text{FLOPs/Byte}\), log scale from \(10^{-1}\) to \(10^4\)).
Y-Axis: Attainable Performance (\(\text{TFLOPs/s}\) or \(\text{GFLOPs/s}\), log scale).
Ridge Point (\(I^* = R_{\text{peak}} / \text{BW}\)): The transition point between memory-bound sloped line (\(P = I \times \text{BW}\)) and horizontal ceiling (\(P = R_{\text{peak}}\)).
Design Point: A diamond marker showing the workload’s current intensity and attainable throughput.




import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

def build_roofline_chart(peak_tflops: float, bandwidth_gbs: float, workload_ai: float):
    # Ridge point
    ridge_ai = (peak_tflops * 1e3) / bandwidth_gbs

    x = np.logspace(-1, 4, 200)
    # Roofline equation: P_attainable = min(peak, AI * BW)
    y_roof = np.minimum(peak_tflops * 1e3, x * bandwidth_gbs) / 1e3 # in TFLOPs/s

    # Attainable performance for active workload
    workload_perf = min(peak_tflops * 1e3, workload_ai * bandwidth_gbs) / 1e3
    regime = "Compute-Bound" if workload_ai >= ridge_ai else "Memory-Bound"

    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x, y=y_roof,
        mode='lines',
        name='Hardware Ceiling',
        line=dict(color='#64748B', width=3),
        fill='tozeroy',
        fillcolor='rgba(241, 245, 249, 0.5)'
    ))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[workload_ai], y=[workload_perf],
        mode='markers+text',
        marker=dict(size=14, color='#A51C30' if regime == "Memory-Bound" else '#1F407A', symbol='diamond'),
        text=[f"Design Point ({regime})"],
        textposition="top center",
        name='Workload'
    ))
    fig.add_vline(x=ridge_ai, line_dash="dot", line_color="#94A3B8", annotation_text=f"Ridge ({ridge_ai:.1f} FLOP/B)")
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis=dict(type='log', title="Arithmetic Intensity (FLOPs/Byte)"),
        yaxis=dict(type='log', title="Attainable Performance (TFLOPs/s)"),
        title=f"Roofline Analysis: {regime} (Ridge = {ridge_ai:.1f} FLOP/B)",
        height=350,
        template="plotly_white",
    )
    return fig

Empirical CDF & Tail-Latency Percentile Curve



go.Scatter(x=..., y=..., mode='lines') plotting sorted query execution latencies against percentiles (\(0\%\) to \(99.9\%\)).



Vital for Serving and MLOps labs (Labs 12, 13, 14). Convinces students that mean latency (\(\mu\)) is an engineering lie—in real-world distributed inference, multi-tenant contention, queueing bursts, and garbage collection produce severe \(p99\) and \(p99.9\) tail spikes that breach service SLAs.




X-Axis: Latency in milliseconds.

SLA Wall: Vertical dashed line indicating the maximum allowable client deadline.




import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

def build_tail_cdf(latencies_ms, sla_budget_ms=25.0):
    sorted_lat = np.sort(latencies_ms)
    p = 100.0 * np.arange(len(sorted_lat)) / (len(sorted_lat) - 1)

    p50 = np.percentile(sorted_lat, 50)
    p95 = np.percentile(sorted_lat, 95)
    p99 = np.percentile(sorted_lat, 99)
    sla_violation_pct = np.mean(sorted_lat > sla_budget_ms) * 100.0

    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=sorted_lat, y=p, mode='lines', name='Empirical CDF', line=dict(color='#1F407A', width=2.5)))
    fig.add_vline(x=sla_budget_ms, line_dash="dash", line_color="#DC2626", annotation_text=f"SLA Ceiling ({sla_budget_ms}ms)")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[p50, p95, p99], y=[50, 95, 99],
        mode='markers+text',
        text=[f"p50: {p50:.1f}ms", f"p95: {p95:.1f}ms", f"p99: {p99:.1f}ms"],
        textposition="top left",
        marker=dict(size=9, color=['#10B981', '#F59E0B', '#EF4444']),
        name='Percentiles'
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Latency Distribution (Tail Violation Rate: {sla_violation_pct:.2f}%)",
        xaxis_title="Inference Latency (ms)",
        yaxis_title="CDF Percentile (%)",
        height=340,
        template="plotly_white",
    )
    return fig

title: MLSysBook Interactive Modes & Tooling Catalog
text:
The MLSysBook interactive curriculum rejects passive notebook reading. Systems engineering cannot be mastered through static code cells or linear prose because systems are defined by coupling, constraints, and non-linear multi-dimensional trade-off spaces.
When an engineer scales batch size, latency does not simply drop; memory spills, cache lines thrash, and queueing delays spike at the 99th percentile. When precision is quantized from FP16 to INT4, memory bandwidth bottlenecks ease, but kernel dequantization overheads arise and catastrophic numerical divergence looms.
To teach this intuition, our Marimo labs adhere to four strict design tenets: 1. Predict Before Observing (Gated Cognitive Friction): Students must record a hypothesis before simulation instrumentation renders. Free-wheeling widget twiddling without prior mental commitment breeds false fluency. 2. Visceral Productive Failure: Hitting a hardware thermal ceiling, an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) panic, or an SLA deadline violation must trigger clear, unignorable feedback (shaking redouts, cliff graphs) that directly exposes the binding physical constraint. 3. Multi-Perspective Grounding (The 4 Archetypes): Every concept is evaluated through four distinct industry archetypes: - Cloud Supercomputing: Scale-out H100/H200 clusters, SLA cliffs, multi-tenant throughput, energy megawatts. - Edge & Embodied AI: NVIDIA Drive Orin / Jetson, sub-10ms hard real-time safety, rare-hazard perception. - Mobile SoC: Apple Silicon / Qualcomm Snapdragon NPU, unified memory, thermal throttling envelopes. - TinyML & Microcontrollers: ARM Cortex-M55 / ESP32-S3, strict <512 KB SRAM limits, micro-watt energy harvesting. 4. Traceable Architectural Accounting: Every design choice updates an immutable Design Ledger, teaching students to defend decisions with empirical telemetry and Iron Law accounting.

Continuous Value Slider



marimo.ui.slider(start, stop, step, value, label, debounce=False)



Use when sweeping through a smooth physical continuum where marginal incremental changes reveal continuous trade-off dynamics (e.g., clock frequency throttling, continuous memory allocation percentage, data drift intensity, operational duty cycle).




start (float): Lower bound of the physical sweep.
stop (float): Upper bound of the physical sweep.
step (float): Fine-grained increment (e.g., 0.1 or 1.0).
value (float): Default baseline setting.
label (str): Descriptive label including physical units (e.g., "Clock Frequency (GHz)", "Data Drift Pressure (%)").
debounce (bool): Set to True if triggering expensive multi-variable Monte Carlo simulations, or False for instant analytical formula updates.




import marimo as mo

# Continuous drift pressure knob affecting the verification gap and accuracy degradation
partA_drift = mo.ui.slider(
    start=0.0,
    stop=100.0,
    step=1.0,
    value=35.0,
    label="Production Drift Rate λ (%/month)",
)







Discrete Step & Power-of-Two Slider



marimo.ui.slider(steps=[...], value=..., label=...)



Use for hardware and architectural parameters that only physically exist in discrete powers of two, standard memory alignments, SIMD vector widths, or quantized bit-widths (e.g., batch size \(B \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128\}\), cache line widths, quantization precision levels).

value (Union[int, float]): Initial default chosen from steps.
label (str): Label indicating discrete systems parameter.




import marimo as mo

# Micro-batch size sweep: changes GEMM operational intensity and memory access patterns
batch_size_knob = mo.ui.slider(
    steps=[1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512],
    value=16,
    label="Inference Micro-Batch Size (B)",

marimo.ui.range_slider(start, stop, step, value=[low, high], label=...)

text:
Dynamic Multi-Objective Pareto Frontier



go.Scatter(x=..., y=..., mode='markers+lines') with convex-hull or non-dominated sorting logic.



Use to demonstrate that in real-world ML systems, there are no unilateral optimizations—only trade-offs along an optimal boundary. Any point below/behind the frontier is sub-optimal; any point beyond it is physically impossible under current technology constraints.




X-Axis: Cost Metric (Latency in ms, Energy in Joules, Dollar Cost $/1M tokens, or SRAM footprint in KB).
Y-Axis: Quality Metric (Top-1 Accuracy %, BLEU/ROUGE score, Safety Margin %).
Marker Color/Size: Secondary trade-off (e.g., Model Parameter Scale or Peak Thermal Dissipation).
Frontier Line: Step-wise or convex hull connecting non-dominated operating configurations.




import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

def build_pareto_frontier(models, active_point):
    # Sort models by latency
    sorted_models = sorted(models, key=lambda m: m['latency_ms'])
    pareto_x, pareto_y = [], []
    max_acc = -1.0
    for m in sorted_models:
        if m['accuracy_pct'] > max_acc:
            pareto_x.append(m['latency_ms'])
            pareto_y.append(m['accuracy_pct'])
            max_acc = m['accuracy_pct']

    fig = go.Figure()
    # Non-dominated frontier
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=pareto_x, y=pareto_y,
        mode='lines',
        name='Pareto Frontier',
        line=dict(color='#A51C30', width=2, dash='dash')
    ))
    # All candidate architectural designs
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[m['latency_ms'] for m in models],
        y=[m['accuracy_pct'] for m in models],
        mode='markers+text',
        text=[m['name'] for m in models],
        textposition='top right',
        marker=dict(size=10, color='#1F407A', opacity=0.7),
        name='Architectural Candidates'
    ))
    # Currently evaluated student design
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[active_point['latency_ms']],
        y=[active_point['accuracy_pct']],
        mode='markers',
        marker=dict(size=16, color='#247A4D', symbol='star', line=dict(width=2, color='white')),
        name='Your Active Design'
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        title="Accuracy vs. Latency Pareto Surface",
        xaxis=dict(title="P99 Inference Latency (ms) [Lower is Better]"),
        yaxis=dict(title="Downstream Task Accuracy (%) [Higher is Better]"),
        template="plotly_white",
        height=380,
    )
    return fig







Williams Operational Roofline Model



go.Scatter(..., x=..., y=..., mode='lines') on dual logarithmic axes (\(\log_{10} - \log_{10}\)) with dynamic design point diamonds.



The foundational visualization for hardware-software co-design (Labs 02, 05, 10, 11). Quantifies whether a workload is Memory-Bandwidth Bound or Peak-Compute Bound based on its Arithmetic Intensity (\(I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{Byte}\)).




X-Axis: Arithmetic Intensity (\(\text{FLOPs/Byte}\), log scale from \(10^{-1}\) to \(10^4\)).
Y-Axis: Attainable Performance (\(\text{TFLOPs/s}\) or \(\text{GFLOPs/s}\), log scale).
Ridge Point (\(I^* = R_{\text{peak}} / \text{BW}\)): The transition point between memory-bound sloped line (\(P = I \times \text{BW}\)) and horizontal ceiling (\(P = R_{\text{peak}}\)).
Design Point: A diamond marker showing the workload’s current intensity and attainable throughput.




import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

def build_roofline_chart(peak_tflops: float, bandwidth_gbs: float, workload_ai: float):
    # Ridge point
    ridge_ai = (peak_tflops * 1e3) / bandwidth_gbs

    x = np.logspace(-1, 4, 200)
    # Roofline equation: P_attainable = min(peak, AI * BW)
    y_roof = np.minimum(peak_tflops * 1e3, x * bandwidth_gbs) / 1e3 # in TFLOPs/s

    # Attainable performance for active workload
    workload_perf = min(peak_tflops * 1e3, workload_ai * bandwidth_gbs) / 1e3
    regime = "Compute-Bound" if workload_ai >= ridge_ai else "Memory-Bound"

    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=x, y=y_roof,
        mode='lines',
        name='Hardware Ceiling',
        line=dict(color='#64748B', width=3),
        fill='tozeroy',
        fillcolor='rgba(241, 245, 249, 0.5)'
    ))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[workload_ai], y=[workload_perf],
        mode='markers+text',
        marker=dict(size=14, color='#A51C30' if regime == "Memory-Bound" else '#1F407A', symbol='diamond'),
        text=[f"Design Point ({regime})"],
        textposition="top center",
        name='Workload'
    ))
    fig.add_vline(x=ridge_ai, line_dash="dot", line_color="#94A3B8", annotation_text=f"Ridge ({ridge_ai:.1f} FLOP/B)")
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis=dict(type='log', title="Arithmetic Intensity (FLOPs/Byte)"),
        yaxis=dict(type='log', title="Attainable Performance (TFLOPs/s)"),
        title=f"Roofline Analysis: {regime} (Ridge = {ridge_ai:.1f} FLOP/B)",
        height=350,
        template="plotly_white",
    )
    return fig







Waterfall Latency & Energy Decomposition Stack



go.Bar with overlay or stacked modes, or go.Waterfall.



Essential for teaching The Iron Law of ML Systems (\(T = T_{\text{mem}} + T_{\text{comp}} + L_{\text{lat}}\)) and Amdahl’s Law. Shows why accelerating compute by \(10\times\) yields only negligible speedup if memory movement or un-fused kernel launches dominate runtime.




Stages: Pre-processing/Tokenization, Memory Transfer (\(D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW}\)), Tensor Core Compute (\(O / (R \cdot \eta)\)), Kernel Launch & Pipeline Overhead (\(L\)).
Ghost Bar: Gray dashed outline of previous un-optimized baseline to immediately reveal deltas.




import plotly.graph_objects as go

def build_latency_waterfall(comp_ms, mem_ms, ovh_ms, prev_breakdown=None):
    stages = ['Compute (GEMM)', 'Memory Traffic (HBM/SRAM)', 'Kernel Launch Overhead']
    current_vals = [comp_ms, mem_ms, ovh_ms]

    fig = go.Figure()
    if prev_breakdown:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
            x=stages, y=prev_breakdown,
            name='Baseline (Pre-Opt)',
            marker=dict(color='rgba(148, 163, 184, 0.3)', line=dict(color='#94A3B8', width=1.5, dash='dash')),
            width=0.5
        ))
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=stages, y=current_vals,
        name='Optimized System',
        marker=dict(color=['#1F407A', '#A51C30', '#D97706']),
        width=0.35
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        title="Iron Law Latency Decomposition Breakdown",
        yaxis=dict(title="Execution Time (ms)"),
        barmode='overlay',
        template="plotly_white",
        height=320,
    )
    return fig







Radar / Spider Multi-Axis System Trade-Off Chart



go.Scatterpolar(r=..., theta=..., fill='toself')



Use when evaluating holistically across conflicting system properties: Compute Efficiency, Memory Footprint Margin, Latency Margin, Downstream Accuracy, Energy Efficiency, and Engineering Dollar Cost.




Radial Coordinates: Normalized scores (\(0\%\) to \(100\%\), where \(100\%\) represents meeting or exceeding the budget).
Threshold Ring: A dashed circle at \(70\%\) or \(100\%\) representing the mandatory production feasibility boundary.




import plotly.graph_objects as go

def build_dam_radar(data_score: float, algo_score: float, machine_score: float, threshold: float = 70.0):
    categories = ['Data Freshness/Coverage', 'Algorithmic Capacity', 'Machine Throughput/HW Envelope']
    # Close the loop
    r_vals = [data_score, algo_score, machine_score, data_score]
    theta_vals = categories + [categories[0]]
    threshold_vals = [threshold, threshold, threshold, threshold]

    fig = go.Figure()
    # Required threshold perimeter
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatterpolar(
        r=threshold_vals, theta=theta_vals,
        mode='lines',
        name='Feasibility Floor',
        line=dict(color='#DC2626', dash='dash', width=2),
    ))
    # Active system profile
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatterpolar(
        r=r_vals, theta=theta_vals,
        fill='toself',
        name='System Readiness',
        fillcolor='rgba(31, 64, 122, 0.25)',
        line=dict(color='#1F407A', width=2),
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        polar=dict(radialaxis=dict(visible=True, range=[0, 100])),
        title="D·A·M Triad System Diagnostic Radar",
        height=350,
        template="plotly_white",
    )
    return fig







2D Design-Space Sweep Heatmap



go.Heatmap(z=..., x=..., y=..., colorscale=...)



Use when exploring the joint interaction of two critical knobs (e.g., Batch Size vs. Sequence Length, or Quantization Bitwidth vs. KV Cache Size). Immediately highlights the Feasibility Cliff (OOM faults or SLA misses).




X-Axis: First control variable.
Y-Axis: Second control variable.
Z-Axis (Color): Latency (ms), Throughput (tok/s), or Memory (GB). Cells violating constraints are highlighted with a distinct hatching or red palette.




import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

def build_feasibility_heatmap(batch_sizes, precisions, memory_limit_gb=80.0):
    # Mock computation of memory allocation
    z_mem = []
    text_labels = []
    for p in precisions:
        row = []
        label_row = []
        b_bytes = 2 if p == "FP16" else (1 if p == "INT8" else 0.5)
        for b in batch_sizes:
            mem = 14.0 + (b * 2048 * 4096 * 32 * 2 * b_bytes) / 1e9 # weights + KV cache
            row.append(mem)
            label_row.append(f"{mem:.1f} GB<br>({'OOM' if mem > memory_limit_gb else 'OK'})")
        z_mem.append(row)
        text_labels.append(label_row)

    fig = go.Figure(data=go.Heatmap(
        z=z_mem,
        x=[f"B={b}" for b in batch_sizes],
        y=precisions,
        text=text_labels,
        texttemplate="%{text}",
        colorscale=[[0, '#10B981'], [0.75, '#F59E0B'], [1.0, '#EF4444']],
        colorbar=dict(title="VRAM (GB)"),
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"VRAM Footprint Surface (Hard Limit: {memory_limit_gb} GB)",
        xaxis_title="Batch Size",
        yaxis_title="Numeric Precision",
        height=340,
        template="plotly_white",
    )

Empirical CDF & Tail-Latency Percentile Curve



go.Scatter(x=..., y=..., mode='lines') plotting sorted query execution latencies against percentiles (\(0\%\) to \(99.9\%\)).



Vital for Serving and MLOps labs (Labs 12, 13, 14). Convinces students that mean latency (\(\mu\)) is an engineering lie—in real-world distributed inference, multi-tenant contention, queueing bursts, and garbage collection produce severe \(p99\) and \(p99.9\) tail spikes that breach service SLAs.




X-Axis: Latency in milliseconds.
Y-Axis: Percentile of requests (\(0.50\) to \(0.999\), often logit or non-linear scale).
SLA Wall: Vertical dashed line indicating the maximum allowable client deadline.




import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

def build_tail_cdf(latencies_ms, sla_budget_ms=25.0):
    sorted_lat = np.sort(latencies_ms)
    p = 100.0 * np.arange(len(sorted_lat)) / (len(sorted_lat) - 1)

    p50 = np.percentile(sorted_lat, 50)
    p95 = np.percentile(sorted_lat, 95)
    p99 = np.percentile(sorted_lat, 99)
    sla_violation_pct = np.mean(sorted_lat > sla_budget_ms) * 100.0

    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=sorted_lat, y=p, mode='lines', name='Empirical CDF', line=dict(color='#1F407A', width=2.5)))
    fig.add_vline(x=sla_budget_ms, line_dash="dash", line_color="#DC2626", annotation_text=f"SLA Ceiling ({sla_budget_ms}ms)")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[p50, p95, p99], y=[50, 95, 99],
        mode='markers+text',
        text=[f"p50: {p50:.1f}ms", f"p95: {p95:.1f}ms", f"p99: {p99:.1f}ms"],
        textposition="top left",
        marker=dict(size=9, color=['#10B981', '#F59E0B', '#EF4444']),
        name='Percentiles'
    ))
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Latency Distribution (Tail Violation Rate: {sla_violation_pct:.2f}%)",
        xaxis_title="Inference Latency (ms)",
        yaxis_title="CDF Percentile (%)",
        height=340,
        template="plotly_white",
    )

text:
What you will do

Read and predict. Meet the situation, see the learning goals and complete route, and predict a consequence before opening an investigation.
Change and compare. Change one condition and inspect the immediate feedback. Explain what improves, what costs more, and what remains uncertain.
Capture and discuss. Keep contrasting evidence, defend a recommendation or hold, and say what would change your mind. Download the discussion to submit through your course’s usual system.

The book explains concepts, TinyTorch builds the machinery, these labs explore design trade-offs, and StaffML practices defending decisions. Each chapter lab develops its own concepts within your continuing project.



Saving your work

Capturing keeps a comparison fixed while you continue experimenting. Saving a discussion is an explicit action; later changes can make that saved evidence stale. The Design Ledger can retain saved decisions when browser storage is available. Keep a downloaded report for a portable record, especially when storage is unavailable. Storage does not synchronize across devices or submit work to your instructor.
LLM assistance can help with hypotheses and drafting. Your claims still need support from the experiment, including its assumptions and limits. Calculation Notes explain the governing models when you want to dig deeper.





Local notebooks and hardware

Browser labs need no local installation. To modify a notebook or run it locally, install the repository dependencies:
python3 -m pip install -r labs/requirements.txt
python3 -m pip install -e mlsysim
cd labs
marimo run vol1/lab_00_introduction.py
Install dependencies and launch once while connected before relying on offline use.

title: Lab Development Protocol
text:
This public stub tracks the release-facing protocol checks that are enforced by the labs test suite.



Every lab must be a valid Marimo app.
Browser labs must include the WASM bootstrap and relative mlsysim wheel path.
Prediction widgets must be structured controls, not free-text prompts.
Interactive widgets must be returned through Marimo dataflow.
Runtime-installed WASM packages must be imported after micropip.install(...).
Labs should render tabbed parts plus a synthesis section.
Labs should save decisions to the Design Ledger where applicable.

Run python3 -m pytest labs/tests/ -v from the repository root for the current automated checks.



A lab should leave students able to defend a design choice under stated constraints. Its calculations support that decision. Completing arithmetic or selecting the correct prediction is not the learning objective.


Read the complete chapter and its concept map. Give each primary concept an explicit disposition: required investigation, explanation within an investigation, optional extension, or reading only, with a reason. Identify the chapter-owned claim and misconception before choosing the interface. The conclusion integrates earlier owners without introducing new concepts.
Treat worked and napkin examples as starting points. Identify which fixed assumption, untested consequence, or missing evidence the lab should open for investigation. A chapter claim can require a new MLSysIM scenario even when the book has no complete worked example for it. Do not invent empirical quality or hardware measurements to complete a lesson.
Specify the changed and fixed conditions, an informative counterexample or limiting case, the teaching instrument, the saved comparison, and a chapter-specific discussion prompt. Choose the instrument for what students need to notice. Include a changed-assumption transfer question and distinguish predicted consequences from observed results. Optional depth must not silently become a completion requirement.



Support an instructor assigning reading, core investigations, a downloaded discussion report, and submission through the course’s existing system. Retain actual predictions, tested settings, outcomes, units, and scenario versions. Keep those captured facts visibly separate from the student’s interpretation. Ask students to explain the mechanism, defend a chosen or rejected alternative, identify uncertainty, and name a useful follow-up experiment.
LLM assistance can be permitted without making unsupported claims acceptable. Assess reasoning tied to the captured evidence, comparable conditions, trade-offs, limitations, and transfer. Do not grade prediction accuracy, agreement with a universal winner, or prose polish as substitutes for understanding. A justified hold or baseline retention can be a sound conclusion. Capture identifiers connect claims to results; they do not prove authorship.
Each substantive part should give students a short experiment:

Predict a consequence before seeing the result. An incorrect prediction should still unlock exploration.
Change a meaningful system choice while holding the comparison workload fixed, or explicitly identify the changed workload.
Compare the baseline and alternative in real units. Show both the benefit and the cost, alongside the constraint that determines feasibility.
Cross a failure boundary and recover when the scenario permits it. Explain why a better headline metric can still produce an unacceptable design.
Save the tested settings and outcomes before making a recommendation. Synthesis should use those saved experiments, including a rejected alternative, a remaining limitation, and a condition for revisiting the choice.

Charts should make the tradeoff visible: a selected point on a curve, a budget boundary, or a comparison of competing outcomes. A table of calculated answers alone does not establish that students explored the design space. Keep formulas and assumptions available in Calculation Notes.




MLSysIM owns physical behavior, reusable scenario assumptions, and registry facts. Notebooks select inputs and render returned results; the lab helper package owns presentation, evidence capture, and reports. Extend MLSysIM when a model is missing instead of implementing another calculator in a notebook or lab helper. Label illustrative scenarios as assumptions rather than measured hardware behavior.
Browser releases must rebuild the MLSysIM and lab-helper wheels from the source being released. A successful native run does not verify a checked-in browser wheel, and structural tests do not establish physical fidelity or teaching quality.



Inspect the rendered lab after unlocking predictions. Exercise controls, check that outputs change, cross and recover from a constraint violation, and switch contexts to verify that predictions and evidence reset appropriately. Inspect both desktop and narrow-screen layouts, including charts, legends, tables, and tab navigation. Report automated checks separately from these observations.

Extend MLSysIM when a model is missing instead of implementing another calculator in a notebook or lab helper. Label illustrative scenarios as assumptions rather than measured hardware behavior.
Browser releases must rebuild the MLSysIM and lab-helper wheels from the source being released. A successful native run does not verify a checked-in browser wheel, and structural tests do not establish physical fidelity or teaching quality.

title: Lab Development Protocol
text: Inspect the rendered lab after unlocking predictions. Exercise controls, check that outputs change, cross and recover from a constraint violation, and switch contexts to verify that predictions and evidence reset appropriately. Inspect both desktop and narrow-screen layouts, including charts, legends, tables, and tab navigation. Report automated checks separately from these observations.
